tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Juan Diego

debates.text: On the morning of 9 December 1531, Juan Diego, by then a widower of about fifty-five, hurried across Tepeyac hill to hear Mass. It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.concern: The Feast of the Immaculate Conception was celebrated on 8 December, not 9 December. The traditional account places Juan Diego's first encounter with the apparition on 9 December, but it does not establish that the Mass he was attending that morning celebrated the feast.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the sentence about the Mass celebrating the feast, or revise it to say that he was traveling to attend religious instruction or Mass.
debates.before: It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.after: He was traveling to attend religious instruction or Mass.

debates.section: A Convert of the Nahua People
debates.text: Born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac
debates.concern: Juan Diego's birth date, birthplace, pre-baptismal name, and conversion date are based largely on later tradition and are not established by contemporary documentary evidence. The article presents several of these details with more historical precision than the surviving evidence warrants.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify these biographical details as traditional or commonly reported rather than documented fact.
debates.before: Born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac, in what is now central Mexico, Juan Diego belonged to the indigenous Nahua people.
debates.after: According to longstanding tradition, Juan Diego was born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac, in what is now central Mexico, and belonged to the indigenous Nahua people.
debates.comment: Adding attribution appropriately frames traditional biography.

debates.text: had him watched
debates.concern: The traditional apparition narrative describes Zumárraga's questioning and request for a sign, but the claim that he had Juan Diego watched is not clearly established and may be an embellishment.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the claim unless a reliable historical source specifically documents it.
debates.before: and had him watched.
debates.comment: Removing an unsupported minor detail is an improvement.

debates.section: Roses in December, and an Image Left Behind
debates.text: fresh Castilian roses growing impossibly out of season
debates.concern: The roses and their identification as Castilian roses belong to the traditional apparition narrative. Presenting the botanical circumstance as an independently established impossibility overstates what can be historically demonstrated.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Attribute the account to the Guadalupe tradition.
debates.before: Though it was winter and nothing should have been blooming, Juan Diego found fresh Castilian roses growing impossibly out of season.
debates.after: According to the traditional account, Juan Diego found fresh Castilian roses blooming on the hill in December.
debates.comment: Framing the miraculous roses as part of the traditional account prevents presenting legend as flat fact.

debates.text: Historians of the period widely credit it with dramatically accelerating the conversion of Mexico's indigenous population
debates.concern: The article makes a broad causal claim about the image's effect on mass conversion and then gives an unsupported figure and chronology for millions of baptisms. The scale, timing, and causes of sixteenth-century conversions are historically complex and should not be reduced to this precise narrative without evidence.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the claims about historians widely crediting the image and millions converting within a few years with a qualified statement about the devotion's later influence.
debates.before: Historians of the period widely credit it with dramatically accelerating the conversion of Mexico's indigenous population in the years that followed.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Albert the Great

debates.before: rather than left to circulate, as it initially had, chiefly through more religiously suspect Arabic and Averroist channels

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Thomas Aquinas

debates.before: His teacher, Albert the Great, famously and correctly predicted that this misjudgment would one day be reversed. He declared that this ox's bellowing would yet be heard throughout the whole world.

debates.comment: The revised version provides a more historically accurate and nuanced account of Aristotelian transmission.

debates.comment: Changing 'the single most influential' to 'one of the most influential' avoids an unprovable superlative while maintaining high praise.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Clare of Assisi

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Edmund the Martyr

debates.section: A Devotion That Outgrew Its Origins
